title: Claude claims it sent an email or made a file. It did not.
summary: Claude will sometimes say it has emailed someone, saved a document or produced a working link when it has done none of those things. Anthropic's own page for it, stating the cause plainly: Claude has no access to any tool that is not explicitly connected - not email, not a word processor, not file transfer - and it invents the capability while trying to be helpful.
who_for: Anyone about to trust Claude with something it says it has already done. The single most expensive first-week mistake, in the publisher's own words rather than a forum thread's.
skip_if: It explains the behaviour and does not tell you how to spot it in the moment, which is the part you actually need: if Claude reports finishing a task you never watched it do, check the thing itself. Also read it as a floor rather than a ceiling - connectors change what Claude really can reach, and this page is about the case where nothing is connected.
teaches: recognise when Claude claims a capability it does not have
know that Claude cannot email, save or transfer files unless a tool is connected
check the artefact rather than the assurance

title: How up-to-date is Claude's training data?
summary: The knowledge cutoff per model, in a table - January 2026 for the current family, back to August 2023 for Opus 3 - with the plain statement that a model may not know about anything after its own date.
who_for: Anyone about to ask Claude about something recent and take the answer at face value. The one fact that explains a whole class of confident wrong answers.
skip_if: It states the limit and offers no way round it: web search, which is the actual answer, is never mentioned. Read it for the dates, then go and turn search on. The page also carries no visible publication date - it says only 'updated this week' - so the cutoffs it lists are current on the day you read it and not before.
teaches: know that each model has a fixed knowledge cutoff
match a model to its cutoff date
expect confident answers about events after the cutoff to be wrong

title: How does Claude handle mathematical equations and calculations?
summary: Claude can work through equations and arithmetic, and Anthropic's own page says complex or mission-critical calculations should be verified with specialist software or by hand.
who_for: Anyone who is about to let Claude do a sum that matters - an invoice, a dose, a budget line - and wants the publisher's position before they do.
skip_if: It is a caution and not a method. It does not tell you to switch on code execution, which is the thing that actually makes Claude compute rather than predict, and it does not show you how to check an answer. Take the warning and get the technique elsewhere.

title: Claude is providing incorrect or misleading responses. What's going on?
summary: Anthropic's own account of why Claude gets things wrong - hallucination, stale training data, quotes that are fabricated but sound authoritative - and three things to do about it: do not make Claude your only source on anything that matters, open the sources it cites, and use the thumbs-down.
who_for: Someone who has just caught Claude being confidently wrong and wants to know whether it is broken or normal. It is normal, and this says so from the publisher.
skip_if: The remedies put the work on you and stop there - verify, check sources, report. Nothing here about prompting to reduce the risk in the first place, and the fabricated-quote warning deserves more than the sentence it gets. Two hundred and fifty words.
teaches: know that a confident wrong answer is an expected failure, not a fault
open the source behind a citation before repeating it
avoid using Claude as a single source on anything consequential

title: How do usage and length limits work?
summary: The two limits people confuse. Usage limits are a message budget over time and depend on the plan; length limits are the context window, described as working memory, at 200K, 500K or 1M tokens depending on the model. When you hit the first you wait, upgrade or buy credits; when you hit the second you start a new conversation or move to a Project.
who_for: Someone who has just been cut off mid-task and cannot tell whether they ran out of messages or out of room. Two different walls, two different answers.
skip_if: It names the token numbers and then sends you to another page for the per-model breakdown, so you will click again. It also gives no way to see how close you are to either limit before you hit it, which is the thing you actually wanted.
teaches: tell a usage limit apart from a context-length limit
know the three context window sizes and what they mean in practice
respond to each limit correctly - wait or upgrade, versus start fresh

what is a context window

title: What are artifacts and how do I use them?
summary: What the side panel is. Claude opens an Artifact when the thing it is making is substantial and stands alone - roughly fifteen lines or more, and something you are likely to edit or reuse. Documents, code, sites, SVG, React. You can edit in place by asking, download the file, keep several at once, publish one, or build one that calls Claude itself.
who_for: Someone who watched a panel open beside the chat and does not know what it is, whether it is saved, or how to get the file out.
skip_if: It runs from 'what is this panel' to publishing an app with persistent storage and MCP in one page, so the last third is aimed at somebody two levels further on. Read the first half. The page also carries no publication date, only 'updated yesterday', so treat the feature list as current on the day you read it.
teaches: recognise when and why Claude opens an Artifact
edit an Artifact by asking rather than by copying it out
download or publish what Claude made
